12. What stays private

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-12-privacy.Rmd
book-12-privacy.Rmd

What you will learn

Distinguish a private assignment from an aggregate release, understand distinct-person support, and recognise refused identifiers and free text.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.questionnaire, the synthetic questionnaire study described there.

Start this chapter

Log in first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.questionnaire", server = "site")$conns

The connection is ready; conns identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

Know which side holds each object

On your computer On each server
Recipe definitions, concept sets and parameters Database records and credentials
Public table/column/vocabulary metadata Pseudonymous person and episode rows
Output symbol names Exact permitted dates, ages and derived columns
Disclosure-checked aggregates Intermediate populations and joins

A symbol is the name of a server object. Seeing the name does not give you its contents. Pseudonymisation replaces person IDs for protected processing; it does not make a patient-level table suitable for download.

private <- omop_recipe(variables = list(age = omop_age_at("2024-06-01"), sex = omop_sex()),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(private, out = c(people = "D_private"), conns = conns)

The reply names D_private, the server table holding age and sex. Exact completed age stays beside the source data; the table is available for approved analysis calls in your DataSHIELD session.

YouChoose events, variables and outputs.
→
ServerCompute with private records and apply release checks.
→
You seeSymbol names, schemas and checked summaries.

Request an aggregate 

dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_private$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#>
#> $site$length
#> [1] 48
#>
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>   5%  10%  25%  50%  75%  90%  95% Mean
#>   34   34   34   43   49   49   49   42
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_private$age", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 12

The mean completed age on 2024-06-01 is 42 years across 36 valid values; 12 people with year-only births have missing completed age. The roster includes all people; a fixed-date age calculation does not establish survival to that date. An approved aggregate method checks its own disclosure rules. A successfully assigned table does not guarantee every later summary or model will be releasable.

Note

A private assignment is not a row download. Every later aggregate uses the disclosure rules of its own method.

The final release rule

Each final patient component needs enough distinct persons for the server’s nfilter.subset. Many events from one person still contribute only one person to this check. Our server sets nfilter.subset = 5, stricter than the dsBase default of 3. Each data owner chooses the server policy.

Rule What it checks Value on this server
nfilter.subset Distinct people in a final assigned patient table 5
nfilter.tab Nonzero cells in a dsBase frequency table 3

These checks apply at different steps. A table with enough people to assign can still produce frequency cells too small to release.

Intermediate calculations may contain small populations privately. The gate is at final publication; a joined result’s private inputs do not need separate published symbols. A standalone filter produces a final object and is gated. Here we intentionally request a subset with no qualifying rows:

ds.omop.filter("D_private", expr = omop_where(age > 200L),
  newobj = "D_too_small", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP filter failed and was rolled back: site: Disclosive: operation blocked - insufficient individuals to meet disclosure threshold. No further details available.; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The refusal reports the policy boundary without providing the small private count. The previous D_private object remains available. Empty and undersized results share this protection; do not interpret the diagnostic as a patient count.

Why identifiers and source text are refused

Class 1 includes direct identifiers, source identifiers and free text that may contain identifiers. Renaming a source field does not make it safe. Both output values and predicates are checked, so a count cannot be used to probe a forbidden text column. The following intentionally invalid definition demonstrates that check:

Fever question is 900002, found in chapter 4.

blocked <- omop_recipe(variables = list(answer = omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L, value = "value_as_string"),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_to_plan(blocked)
#> Error:
#> ! Disclosive: the plan requests blocked (class-1) column(s) that the server can never release or filter on: value_as_string (event 'obs_900002' value).

This definition is refused before execution. Use the reviewed coded answer value_as_concept_id and translated categories when it answers the question, as in chapter 10. Free text is not needed for that analysis.

Why dates and ages can remain private columns

Class 2 means a quasi-identifier: a value that may help identify someone when combined with other facts. Exact dates, birth components and ages are permitted in private server tables. Their aggregates and any category labels still face the applicable release controls.

date_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(visit_date = omop_date("first_visit")),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(date_recipe, out = c(people = "D_private_date"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_private_date", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"  "visit_date"

The schema shows person_id and visit_date; it does not reveal the dates. Turning an exact date into a factor publishes category labels as metadata, which needs its own support checks. A fine custom date pattern can therefore be refused even when a private Date column is permitted. Coarsen to the scientifically appropriate month/quarter/year and request an approved aggregate; do not encode a disallowed field into another name or type.

Protected keys cannot become analyst variables 

ds.omop.mutate("D_private", copied = person_id,
  newobj = "D_key_copy", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP mutate failed and was rolled back: site: validation_error: omopMutateDS: column 'person_id' is a protected identifier and cannot be used in an expression; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The server needs keys to align rows and joins; an analyst mutation cannot copy, rewrite or filter them. Use the declared population and join operations instead.

What the disclosure checks mean

Class 3 covers ordinary analytic values, such as coded categories and numeric measurements, rather than identifiers. It does not mean “safe to download”: these values still remain private and their aggregates face release checks. The analyses in this book use DataSHIELD disclosure controls and add no noise. Some OHDSI analysis routes add noise fixed for each request, so repeating the same request returns the same answer.

Exercise 1: a nonempty subset can also be too small

Keep female participants whose completed age is 43 on the declared date. The public questionnaire description places four people in this group. Predict whether the server can assign that final subset.

Solution

ds.omop.filter("D_private", expr = omop_where(age == 43 & sex == "F"),
  newobj = "D_small_group", conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! OMOP filter failed and was rolled back: site: Disclosive: operation blocked - insufficient individuals to meet disclosure threshold. No further details available.; There are some DataSHIELD errors, list them with datashield.errors().

The four-person group is below nfilter.subset = 5, so it is refused just as the empty group was. The message does not disclose the small count; here the count was known from the public teaching data. In a real study, retain a scientifically justified larger population or report that the intended analysis cannot be released.

Exercise 2: did a refused copy create a table?

After the protected-key refusal, list the server objects. Is D_key_copy present?

Solution

DSI::datashield.symbols(conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "D_private"      "D_private_date" "omop"

D_private and D_private_date still exist, but D_key_copy, D_too_small and D_small_group are absent. A refused request did not create a usable table. A schema or object name is metadata, not access to its patient rows.

Recap

A recipe creates private objects and returns their names. Final patient outputs need distinct-person support; aggregates and category metadata have further checks. Class-1 fields and protected-key expressions are refused.
